research_text:
## Research brief

### 1. Governed API and meaning of the reported value

`java.security.MessageDigest` is the Java Cryptography Architecture engine class for computing a message digest: an arbitrary-length input is processed into a fixed-length hash value. The documented lifecycle is: obtain an implementation with `getInstance`, supply data through one or more `update` calls (or use `digest(byte[])` for the final update), then call a `digest` method to complete the computation. A digest call resets the object to its initialized state. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/MessageDigest.html))

For this CrySL rule, the reported value **MD5** refers to the `algorithm` argument captured at the `MessageDigest.getInstance` factory event—not to a byte passed to `update`, the input of `digest(byte[])`, a returned digest, or a comparison result. The rule binds `algorithm` only in its two `getInstance` event patterns and constrains that value to its SHA-2 allow-list. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/MessageDigest.crysl))

This is therefore an **algorithm-membership rule result**: MD5 is not among the rule file’s allowed algorithm strings. It is not, from this rule alone, a statement about the purpose of the digest, whether a digest comparison supplies integrity/authentication, runtime reachability, or the safety of a particular persisted or external contract.

**Important discrepancy:** the detector text supplied in the question lists both hyphenated and unhyphenated spellings (`SHA-256` and `SHA256`, etc.). The verified `MessageDigest.crysl` source itself lists **only** `"SHA-256"`, `"SHA-384"`, and `"SHA-512"` in its algorithm constraint. The rule source does not explain why the detector message also displays aliases. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/MessageDigest.crysl))

---

### 2. Documented correct usage, safe algorithm guidance, and remediation limits

#### Java API semantics

The official Java documentation specifies the following relevant use:

- `MessageDigest.getInstance(String algorithm)` requests an implementation of the named digest algorithm from the first suitable registered provider; it throws `NoSuchAlgorithmException` if none supports that algorithm. The provider-taking overloads request a particular provider. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/MessageDigest.html))
- Standard Java security algorithm names are case-insensitive. Oracle’s JCA guide says applications should use standard names rather than provider-specific aliases, because aliases need not be implemented consistently by every provider. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/javase/8/docs/technotes/guides/security/crypto/CryptoSpec.html))
- Data is supplied with `update`; `digest()` completes the computation; and `digest(byte[])` is documented as performing `update(input)` followed by `digest()`. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/MessageDigest.html))
- `MessageDigest.isEqual` is documented only as digest equality comparison, with an implementation note on the bytes examined and timing dependence. The API does **not** document that use of this equality method establishes an authentication or integrity protocol. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/MessageDigest.html))

The Java standard-name specification recognizes both `MD5` and SHA-family names as names that may be passed to `MessageDigest`; recognition as a standard name is not an endorsement of MD5 for every security purpose. It specifies that MD5 produces a 128-bit digest, while SHA-256, SHA-384, and SHA-512 produce 256-, 384-, and 512-bit digests, respectively. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/specs/security/standard-names.html))

#### Safe-algorithm guidance available from primary sources

The Java `MessageDigest` API itself does **not** provide a security policy that says “replace MD5 with algorithm X,” nor does it provide a migration procedure for MD5. The applicable policy in the reviewed rule is the rule’s allow-list, not a JDK runtime prohibition.

For uses that require a secure hash algorithm, NIST states that the SHA-2 family—including SHA-256, SHA-384, and SHA-512—may be used for applications employing secure hash algorithms, and encourages SHA-256 at minimum where interoperability is required. NIST also states that SHA-2 hash functions are acceptable for all hash-function applications in its SP 800-131A Rev. 2 guidance. ([csrc.nist.gov](https://csrc.nist.gov/projects/hash-functions/nist-policy-on-hash-functions))

**Bounded remediation conclusion:** Where the digest use actually requires a secure hash function and changing the external representation is permitted, the primary-source-aligned replacement family is SHA-2, with the CrySL rule specifically accepting the standard spellings `SHA-256`, `SHA-384`, or `SHA-512`. The sources reviewed do **not** establish that every MD5 use has that security purpose, and they do not prescribe replacement of an unchanged external MD5 contract.

NIST’s description of a MAC is explicitly different: a MAC uses a cryptographic key and can provide data-integrity and source-authentication assurance. Nothing in the supplied finding identifies a `Mac` operation, a key, or a protocol construction; no such conclusion should be drawn from a digest equality comparison alone. ([nvlpubs.nist.gov](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/SpecialPublications/NIST.SP.800-131Ar2.pdf))

---

### 3. Compatibility, formats, platform support, and migration documentation

#### Persisted and wire formats

The reviewed Java API documentation returns digest values as `byte[]`; it does not define a serialization format, text encoding (hex/base64), record layout, version marker, database schema, or wire-protocol migration format. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/MessageDigest.html))

A direct consequence of the documented output lengths is that an MD5 value is 128 bits, while SHA-256/SHA-384/SHA-512 values are 256/384/512 bits. **This implies** that raw stored or transmitted digest fields, and encoded representations derived from them, generally differ in length and value after an algorithm change. This is an inference from the documented digest lengths; the Java API supplies no compatibility layer or automatic translation between digest algorithms. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/specs/security/standard-names.html))

Accordingly, the official sources reviewed provide **no documented migration path** for:

- accepting legacy MD5 persisted values while writing SHA-2 values;
- negotiating a digest algorithm over a wire format;
- tagging values with an algorithm identifier;
- dual-reading or backfilling existing records; or
- preserving compatibility with an external MD5 contract.

Those questions require evidence about the relevant data format or protocol; that evidence is not present in the reported rule result.

#### Platform and provider support

Support has both Java-platform-version and provider dimensions:

- Java SE 8 documentation states that every implementation is required to support `MD5`, `SHA-1`, and `SHA-256`; it directs users to release documentation for additional algorithms. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/javase/8/docs/api/java/security/MessageDigest.html))
- The current Java SE 25 `MessageDigest` documentation states required support for `SHA-1`, `SHA-256`, and `SHA-384`, and likewise directs users to implementation release documentation for algorithms beyond that listed set. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/MessageDigest.html))
- Oracle’s JDK 8 `SUN` provider documentation lists SHA-256, SHA-384, and SHA-512 as supported `MessageDigest` algorithms. This establishes support for that documented Oracle JDK 8 provider, not for every Java runtime/provider combination. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/javase/8/docs/technotes/guides/security/SunProviders.html))
- Oracle’s JCA documentation advises general-purpose applications not to request a specific provider unless it is known to be available, because provider-specific requests reduce portability. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/javase/8/docs/technotes/guides/security/crypto/CryptoSpec.html))

**Unresolved compatibility question:** no target Java release, actual provider set, persisted-format definition, peer protocol, or external contract was supplied. Therefore the sources cannot determine whether SHA-384/SHA-512 are available in the target deployment or whether a format change is compatible.

---

### 4. Exact verified CrySL rule content and matching scope

**Verified source URL:**  
`https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/MessageDigest.crysl`

The file scopes the rule to this API type. The matching scope clause, quoted verbatim, is:

```text
SPEC java.security.MessageDigest
```

The relevant event declarations, quoted verbatim, are:

```text
g1: getInstance(algorithm);
g2: getInstance(algorithm, _);
Get := g1 | g2;

u1: update(preInputByte);
u2: update(preInput);
u3: update(preInput, preOffset, preLen);
u4: update(preInputByteBuffer);
Update := u1 | u2 | u3 | u4;
d1: output = digest();
d2: output = digest(input);
d3: digest(output, offset, len);
DWOU := d2;
DWU := d1 | d3;
Digest := DWU | DWOU;
```

([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/MessageDigest.crysl))

#### Methods, type, and parameter patterns stated by the file

- **Governed type:** `java.security.MessageDigest`.
- **Factory method patterns:** `getInstance(algorithm)` and `getInstance(algorithm, _)`.
  - The first pattern has one captured parameter named `algorithm`.
  - The second has a first captured parameter named `algorithm` and a second wildcard parameter `_`.
- **Update method patterns:** `update(byte-like input)`, `update(byte-array-like input)`, `update(input, offset, length)`, and `update(ByteBuffer-like input)`, represented by the four names shown above.
- **Digest method patterns:** `digest()`, `digest(input)`, and `digest(output, offset, len)`.

The source then states this event order:

```text
Get, (DWOU | (Update+, Digest))+
```

and these constraints:

```text
algorithm in {"SHA-256", "SHA-384", "SHA-512"};
length[preInput] >= preLen + preOffset;
preOffset >= 0;
preLen > 0;
length[output] >= len + offset;
offset >= 0;
len > 0;
```

([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/MessageDigest.crysl))

Thus, the condition relevant to the MD5 finding is exactly:

```text
algorithm in {"SHA-256", "SHA-384", "SHA-512"};
```

It is the only algorithm condition in the file. The remaining conditions concern offset/length values for the three-argument `update` and `digest` patterns. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/MessageDigest.crysl))

**Can it match a method merely because the method has the same name?** **No, not according to the scope stated in this file.** The file declares `SPEC java.security.MessageDigest`; it does not contain a separate name-only rule for arbitrary classes having methods named `getInstance`, `update`, or `digest`. The source does not further describe the detector’s type-resolution implementation, subtype handling, or behavior for unresolved calls, so no stronger statement about scanner mechanics is supported by this source alone. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/MessageDigest.crysl))

---

## Source limitations

1. The CrySL URL is a mutable `master`-branch URL. The exact rule revision bundled with the reporting detector was not supplied, so identity with the detector’s packaged rule cannot be established from this source alone.
2. The finding message identifies an algorithm-policy mismatch but does not provide a complete call trace, receiver-resolution record, target JDK/provider version, or runtime configuration.
3. Oracle JDK provider documentation establishes availability for the documented Oracle provider/version, not universal support by all Java distributions or installed providers.
4. No primary source reviewed supplies a `MessageDigest`-specific persisted-data, wire-protocol, or dual-format migration procedure.
